_meta.description: Geographic resource & cost factors for the transition. The global learning-curve LCOEs (learning_curves.json) are world averages; these per-zone multipliers scale them so the L2 cost crossover happens at the RIGHT TIME for the location — a watt in Texas/MENA is far cheaper than in Northern Europe or Japan, so those regions strand fossil assets earlier and produce green steel/ammonia/cement more cheaply. Three multiplier channels: clean power (solar/wind/storage), green hydrogen & H2-linked green commodities (H2-DRI steel, green ammonia, SAF), and fossil generation/fuel (gas & coal price differ by region).
_meta.how_used: learning_curves._project_cost multiplies a technology's projected cost by its zone factor before the incumbent-vs-challenger comparison, so find_crossover_year and compute_stranding are region-aware. A factor <1 = cheaper here = earlier crossover.
_meta.calibration: Renewable/H2 factors follow IRENA regional LCOE dispersion (best resource ~US$0.03/kWh solar in MENA/sunbelt/Chile/Australia; ~US$0.06-0.09 in N.Europe/Japan/Korea). Fossil factors follow regional gas/coal price levels (cheap US/MENA/Australia gas; expensive imported LNG in NE Asia and post-2022 Europe). NA-other/global average is the 1.0 reference, so the world-average curves and the documented worked-example anchors are unchanged.

na_sunbelt.label: N. America Sunbelt (generic)
na_sunbelt.resource: excellent solar + wind, cheap land & gas

na_other.label: USA (national average) / Canada
na_other.resource: national/global-average reference — use a sub-national code (e.g. USA-TX) for resolution

us_texas.label: US — Texas (ERCOT)
us_texas.resource: world-class wind + strong solar, cheap land, cheap gas, deregulated market

us_california.label: US — California (CAISO)
us_california.resource: good solar but high land/soft costs & power prices; aggressive policy

us_southeast.label: US — Southeast (FL/GA/…)
us_southeast.resource: moderate solar, very cheap gas, regulated utilities

us_northeast.label: US — Northeast (NY/New England)
us_northeast.resource: poorer onshore resource, high cost, expensive gas; offshore-wind build-out

eu_north.label: N. Europe (DE / Benelux / France)
eu_north.resource: moderate solar, good offshore wind, high cost & gas

eu_uk_ireland.label: UK & Ireland
eu_uk_ireland.resource: world-class offshore wind, weak solar, high gas import cost

eu_nordic.label: Nordics
eu_nordic.resource: abundant cheap hydro + wind; low-carbon grid already

eu_iberia.label: Iberia (Spain / Portugal)
eu_iberia.resource: excellent solar + wind — Europe's cheapest green power & H2

eu_east.label: Central/Eastern Europe (PL/CZ/…)
eu_east.resource: moderate solar, coal-heavy grid, lower labour cost

india.label: India
india.resource: strong solar, low cost, coal-heavy grid

ssa.resource: good resource offset by high cost of capital / execution risk

northeast_asia.label: Japan / Korea / Taiwan
northeast_asia.resource: poor resource, land-constrained, expensive LNG imports

tech_factor_map._note: Which zone factor scales each technology. Unlisted technologies get 1.0 (no geographic dispersion modelled).
tech_factor_map._fossil_note: Only REGIONALLY-PRICED fossil energy carries a geographic factor — natural gas and grid electricity. Globally-traded commodities (coking coal, crude oil, and the coal/oil-based incumbents blast_furnace, cement_clinker, oil_refining, jet_fuel, bunker_fuel) are ~globally priced, so they stay at 1.0 and the green challenger's regional cost drives the crossover (green steel is earliest where clean power / green H2 is cheapest — the intuitive result).

subnational_to_zone._note: Sub-national resolution for the highest-importance markets (US, and finer Europe). Enter the entity's region as an ISO3-prefixed code, e.g. USA-TX, USA-CA, ESP-S. Falls back to the country zone (then global) if not listed. State codes map to their grid/resource region; USA-SW/MW/NE/SE/NW/W are shorthand for the regional zones.
